text.p: Riot engulfed Bulgaria's parliament on Friday as anti-government protesters stormed the building and opposition deputies launched a sit-in to demand a general election.
Dozens of demonstrators forced their way into the building. Police fought them back, spraying them with tear gas and water and barricading the corridors with tables and chairs.

Some 50,000 people were massed outside blowing whistles and burning red flags and effigies representing the ruling Socialist Party, which is in the midst of an economic crisis and a leadership upheaval.
All windows were smashed on the ground floor of the building, a Renaissance-style landmark in the centre of Sofia.
Police trained jets of water down on to crowds who were smashing and overturning the cars which deputies had parked outside.

President-elect Petar Stoyanov -- an opposition figure whose election two months ago marked the collapse of public support for the Socialists -- was overcome by teargas while trying to calm the crowds through a loudspeaker. He was taken away by bodyguards.

Some 200 Interior Ministry troops were brought in to guard the doors of parliament but Socialist deputies dared not leave and opposition members declared they would stay until the Socialists agreed to pass a "salvation declaration" demanding an election.

"We will remain in parliament to press for an early general election as this is the only way out of the crisis," Yordan Sokolov, leader of the Union of Democratic Forces, the main opposition group, told Darik radio, a non-government station.
"What is happening in and outside parliament is the justified wrath of people brought to desperation," he added.
Ambulances took away protesters and policemen who collapsed from tear gas. One hospital said it was treating 15 injured with more still arriving.
Demonstrators blocked narrow streets nearby and pelted any Socialist deputy who tried to step outside with chunks of ice.
People were bringing hot drinks and food for the opposition supporters. Nearby art galleries handed out free coffee and tea.

The government issued an appeal for calm, urging citizens "not to give way to provocations in the name of preserving social peace." The Interior Ministry called for dialogue to resolve tensions but said it would do everything necessary "within the law".
"I hope there is enough common sense not to impose a state of emergency," said Union of Democratic Forces deputy Filip Dimitrov, a former prime minister .
A quarter of Bulgaria's banks are in receivership and triple-digit inflation has slashed real incomes.
On Wednesday the Socialists nominated Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the party's strongman, as prime minister in place of Zhan Videnov, who resigned unexectedly on December 21.
Dobrev was prevented from leaving parliament by a volley of snowballs.
The opposition says the Socialists have failed to tackle the economic crisis and now lack support to form a government.
Voters delivered a powerful no-confidence vote two months ago by electing opposition candidate Stoyanov as president with a 60 percent majority.
The lev collapsed at 660 to the dollar on Friday, from 70 a year ago. It has lost 35 percent of its value against the dollar since the beginning of the year.
"The BSP which led the country to its gravest crisis in history has no right to rule," said Sokolov.

As soon as parliament appoints a new cabinet the International Monetary Fund plans to negotiate implementaton of a tough fixed exchange regime as a last resort to restore confidence in the crumbling economy.
